note: Named individuals. NOT historian-reviewed. Dates for the Chola rulers follow the conventional regnal chronology; dates for saints and poets are frequently traditional rather than established, and are marked with a low certainty and dispute:true where scholarship is divided. Nothing here should be cited.

provenance.SOURCED: Named in an inscription or a text, with the attribution generally accepted.
provenance.DERIVED: The person is attested but the detail here (a date, a relationship) is inferred.
provenance.SYNTHESIZED: Generated. The RECORD is real — the Thanjavur inscription really does list 400 temple women — but the individual is invented to fill a sourced count.
provenance.ABSENT: Known to have existed and not recoverable.

roles.patron: Endows. Often a queen, a merchant guild, or a village assembly.
roles.saint: A devotional figure with a following that outlives them.
roles.architect: Sthapati. Names appear in temple inscriptions.
roles.performer: Dancer, singer, drummer. The Thanjavur inscription lists hundreds.
roles.scribe: Copies. The corpus depends on them and the record almost never names them.

people.name: Vijayalaya Chola
people.note: Took Thanjavur from the Muttaraiyar and began the Chola revival.

people.name: Aditya I
people.note: Absorbed the Pallavas. Built temples along the Kaveri.

people.name: Parantaka I
people.note: The Uttaramerur inscriptions describing election by lot date to his reign.

people.name: Sembiyan Mahadevi
people.note: Queen, mother of Uttama Chola, and the most prolific temple patron of the tenth century in her own right — she rebuilt in stone what had been built in brick, and her endowments are inscribed under her own name.

people.name: Uttama Chola
people.note: Audit procedure for temple accounts is documented under his reign.

people.name: Rajaraja I
people.note: Ordered the great land survey, built the Brihadeeswarar temple, and had its endowments — every donor, every servant, every lamp — cut into its walls.

people.name: Kundavai
people.note: Rajaraja's elder sister. Endowed temples and a hospital, and her gifts are recorded under her own name rather than her brother's.

people.name: Lokamahadevi
people.note: Rajaraja's chief queen; a shrine at Thanjavur carries her name.

people.name: Kunjaramallan Rajaraja Perunthachan
people.note: The sthapati named in the Thanjavur inscriptions. It is unusually rare for the record to name the builder rather than only the patron.

people.name: Karuvur Devar
people.note: Associated with the consecration of the Thanjavur temple; the traditional account is later than the events.

people.name: Nambi Andar Nambi
people.note: Recovered and arranged the Tevaram hymns under Rajaraja. An act of corpus rescue three centuries after composition.

people.name: Rajendra I
people.note: Marched to the Ganga, founded Gangaikonda Cholapuram, and sent a fleet against Srivijaya.

people.name: Krishnan Raman
people.note: A senapati named in Rajaraja's inscriptions.

people.name: Chudamanivarman
people.note: Srivijayan king. The Leiden plates record a Buddhist vihara built for him at Nagapattinam, on Chola land — trade and religion moving together.

people.name: Rajadhiraja I
people.note: Died on the field at Koppam.

people.name: Rajendra II
people.note: Chola inscriptions.

people.name: Virarajendra
people.note: Endowed a college at Ennayiram — a vedic school with a documented student roll.

people.name: Kulottunga I
people.note: Sungam Tavirtta — 'he who abolished tolls'. United the Chola and Eastern Chalukya lines, and sent seventy-two merchants as an embassy to the Song court.

people.name: Ramanuja
people.note: The traditional 120-year lifespan is not credible as given; the figure and the school are firmly attested, the dates are not.

people.name: Yamunacharya
people.note: Traditional dates. Srivaishnava lineage predecessor to Ramanuja.

people.name: Nathamuni
people.note: Credited with recovering and arranging the Alvar hymns. Traditional dates are impossible as stated.

people.name: Vikrama Chola
people.note: Chola inscriptions and court poetry.

people.name: Kulottunga II
people.note: Chola inscriptions and the Periya Puranam colophon tradition.

people.name: Sekkizhar
people.note: Chief minister and author of the Periya Puranam, the lives of the Nayanars — hagiography commissioned by the state.

people.name: Ottakoothar
people.note: Court poet across three reigns.

people.name: Jayamkondar
people.note: Kalingattuparani — war poetry as court literature, and a rare contemporary account of a campaign.

people.name: Kambar
people.note: Dating is contested across two centuries. The Kamba Ramayanam is not a translation but a rival.

people.name: Rajaraja II
people.note: Built Airavatesvara at Darasuram.

people.name: Kulottunga III
people.note: Chola inscriptions.

people.name: Rajaraja III
people.note: Chola inscriptions of a much reduced kingdom.

people.name: Rajendra III
people.note: The last Chola.

people.name: Manikkavachakar
people.note: Tiruvasagam. Dated anywhere from the 6th to the 9th century.

people.name: Andal
people.note: The one woman among the twelve Alvars.

people.name: Ilango Adigal
people.note: Traditionally a Chera prince. The attribution is late and doubted.

people.name: Tiruvalluvar
people.note: Dated across six centuries by different scholars. Almost nothing about the person is recoverable.

people.name: Auvaiyar
people.note: The name belongs to more than one poet across many centuries.

people.name: Panini
people.note: 3,959 generative rules. Endow him and you collect through every grammarian for two thousand years.

people.name: Patanjali
people.note: The Mahabhashya, and its citation by every later grammarian.

people.name: Gargi Vachaknavi
people.note: Argues with Yajnavalkya in open assembly in the Brihadaranyaka, and is not dismissed.

people.name: Kautilya
people.note: The Arthashastra is a composite text compiled over centuries; the single-author attribution is traditional.

people.name: Ashoka
people.note: The only ancient Indian ruler whose own voice survives, because he had it carved on rock. The Maski edict names him personally.

people.name: Mahinda
people.note: Carried the canon to Sri Lanka, where it was written down at Aluvihare two centuries later and survived everything that happened on the mainland.

people.name: Nagarjuna
people.note: His works and the Madhyamaka commentarial tradition.

people.name: Vasubandhu
people.note: The Abhidharmakosha survives in full only because it reached Tibet and China. The Sanskrit was recovered in the twentieth century.

people.name: Buddhaghosa
people.note: The Visuddhimagga and the Sri Lankan chronicle tradition.

people.name: Aryabhata
people.note: Dates himself in the text — he was 23 in 499 — which is why his date is one of the firmest in this list.

people.name: Varahamihira
people.note: His own works and their citation by later astronomers.

people.name: Brahmagupta
people.note: Zero becomes a number with rules. Reached Baghdad in 771 and did not stop travelling.

people.name: Banabhatta
people.note: The Harshacharita and Kadambari, and the Harsha court record.

people.name: Xuanzang
people.note: Studied at Nalanda and left with 657 texts. A one-man redundancy operation, five and a half centuries before the fire.

people.name: Dandin
people.note: Indian poetics as an export good — the Kavyadarsha was translated into Tibetan, Sinhala and Kannada.

people.name: Adi Shankara
people.note: Founded four mathas — institutions designed from the start to outlive their founder, which is why they did.

people.name: Anandavardhana
people.note: The Dhvanyaloka and its Kashmiri commentarial tradition.

people.name: Abhinavagupta
people.note: His own extensive corpus, which names his teachers.

people.name: Kalhana
people.note: The first Indian work that is recognisably history: sources weighed, informants named, predecessors criticised.

people.name: Bhaskara II
people.note: The Lilavati and Siddhanta Shiromani, with a dated colophon tradition.

people.name: Mahavira
people.note: The mathematician, under Rashtrakuta patronage. Not the Jain tirthankara.

people.name: Vijnaneshwara
people.note: The Mitakshara became the standard commentary on Hindu law across most of the subcontinent.

people.name: Basava
people.note: The Anubhava Mantapa: an assembly where artisans and washerwomen argued theology and the record kept their words.

people.name: Akka Mahadevi
people.note: The vachana corpus attributed to her and the Sharana record.

people.name: Pampa
people.note: First of the three gems of Kannada.

people.name: Nannaya
people.note: Telugu literature begins, under Rajaraja Narendra of Vengi.

people.name: Rani Rudrama Devi
people.note: Ruled the Kakatiyas in her own name, and issued inscriptions under a male regnal title as well as her own.

people.name: Jayadeva
people.note: The Gita Govinda and the Sena court tradition.

people.name: Atisha Dipankara
people.note: Left Vikramashila for Tibet in 1042. Fifty years later Vikramashila was ash and what he carried was not.

people.name: Gopala
people.note: Elected king by an assembly of chiefs, according to the Pala tradition — an unusual founding story for a dynasty.

people.name: Dharmapala
people.note: Founded Vikramashila and Somapura.

people.name: Hemachandra
people.note: Jain polymath. Jain merchant capital funded the bhandara libraries that preserved much of what survives from western India.

people.name: Rudradaman I
people.note: The Junagadh inscription: the first long inscription in Sanskrit, and it is mostly about repairing a dam.

people.name: Kharavela
people.note: The Hathigumpha inscription. Its dating is contested by more than a century.

people.name: Lalitaditya Muktapida
people.note: Kalhana’s account and the Martand temple.

people.name: Suyya
people.note: An engineer, named by Kalhana, who drained the Jhelum floods and reordered the valley's fields.

people.name: Sukaphaa
people.note: Crossed the Patkai and founded the Ahom kingdom, which kept written chronicles — the buranjis — as state practice.

people.name: Bhaskaravarman
people.note: Xuanzang visited his court.

people.name: Madhava of Sangamagrama
people.note: Infinite series for pi, sine and cosine — with proofs — two centuries before Europe.

people.name: Nilakantha Somayaji
people.note: The Tantrasangraha, which is dated.

people.name: Jyesthadeva
people.note: The Yuktibhasha, which names its lineage.

people.name: Al-Biruni
people.note: Learned Sanskrit to read the sources, and said so.

people.name: Somadeva
people.note: The Kathasaritsagara and its Kashmiri court dedication.

cohorts.name: Talicceri pendugal of the Rajarajesvaram
cohorts.note: The Thanjavur inscription settles 400 temple women on named streets around the temple, each with a share of land, and lists them individually. The COUNT and the practice are sourced. The individuals this game generates are not those women — they are stand-ins, because reproducing a real list of named people as game characters is a decision for a historian and a community, not for a generator.

cohorts.name: Musicians, drummers and singers of the Rajarajesvaram
cohorts.note: The inscription lists temple servants by function — drummers, conch-blowers, singers of the Tevaram, dance masters, accountants, lamp-lighters, tailors, a potter, an astrologer. The exact total depends on how you count.

cohorts.name: The variyam committees of Uttaramerur
cohorts.note: The inscription sets out eligibility, term limits, disqualification for unaudited accounts, and selection by drawing palm-leaf tickets from a pot. It describes the PROCEDURE in detail and does not preserve a roll of names.

cohorts.name: The Ayyavole Five Hundred
cohorts.note: A merchant guild with its own charter, operating from Java to the Persian Gulf. 'Five hundred' is a title, not a census.
